p.src: Now Jiang Wei gave the order to withdraw. Liao Hua said, “As the saying goes, ‘When a general is in the field, there are commands from his sovereign that he need not obey.’ Though an edict has now arrived, we should not move yet.” Zhang Yi said, “The people of Shu resent the Grand General for campaigning year after year. We would do better to take advantage of this victory, bring our men and horses home, set the people’s minds at ease, and then devise a sound plan anew.” Jiang Wei said, “Well spoken.” He ordered every division to withdraw according to the prescribed formation. He commanded Liao Hua and Zhang Yi to cover the rear and guard against pursuit by the Wei army.

p.src: Meanwhile, Deng Ai led his troops in pursuit, but saw ahead that the banners of the Shu army remained in perfect order and that its men and horses were withdrawing at an unhurried pace. Deng Ai sighed and said, “Jiang Wei has truly mastered the Marquis of Wu’s methods!” Therefore he dared pursue no farther, but reined in his army and returned to the camp at Mount Qi.

p.src: Jiang Wei, upon reaching Chengdu, entered the palace to see the Latter Emperor and asked why he had been recalled. The Latter Emperor said, “You had long remained on the frontier without bringing the army home. Fearing that the soldiers would become exhausted, We issued an edict recalling you to court. We had no other intention.” Jiang Wei said, “Your servant had already taken the camp at Mount Qi and was on the point of completing the victory, yet unexpectedly the undertaking was abandoned halfway. We must surely have fallen victim to Deng Ai’s scheme of sowing discord.” The Latter Emperor remained silent. Jiang Wei memorialized again, “Your servant has sworn to punish the rebels and repay the grace of the state. Your Majesty must not heed the words of petty men and thereby give rise to doubts.” Only after a long while did the Latter Emperor say, “We do not doubt you. For now, return to Hanzhong. When some upheaval arises in Wei, you may campaign against it again.” Jiang Wei left the court sighing and went straight back to Hanzhong.

p.src: Meanwhile, Dang Jun returned to the camp at Mount Qi and reported what had happened. Deng Ai said to Sima Wang, “When sovereign and minister are at odds, internal upheaval is certain to follow.” He then ordered Dang Jun to go to Luoyang and report the matter to Sima Zhao. Sima Zhao was delighted and conceived the desire to conquer Shu. He asked Jia Chong, Protector-General of the Central Army, “What if I attack Shu now?” Jia Chong replied, “You must not attack yet. The Son of Heaven is presently suspicious of my lord; if you rashly leave the capital, trouble will surely break out within. Last year, yellow dragons appeared twice in a well at Ningling. The ministers submitted congratulations, taking them for auspicious signs. But the Son of Heaven said, ‘This is no auspicious sign. The dragon symbolizes the sovereign; yet instead of being above in heaven or below in the fields, it is confined within a well. p.src: It was the fourth month of summer in the fifth year of Ganlu in Wei. Sima Zhao entered the audience hall wearing his sword, and Cao Mao rose to receive him. All the ministers memorialized, “The Grand General’s merit and virtue are magnificent. It is fitting that he be created Duke of Jin and granted the Nine Bestowments.” Cao Mao lowered his head and made no answer. Sima Zhao demanded sternly, “My father, my brothers, and I—three men—have rendered great service to Wei. Can it possibly be improper that I should now become Duke of Jin?” Cao Mao could only reply, “How would I dare disobey?” Sima Zhao said, “In your poem ‘The Hidden Dragon,’ you regard us as no better than loaches and eels. What manner of propriety is that?” Cao Mao could not answer. Sima Zhao gave a cold laugh and descended from the hall. All the officials trembled with fear. Cao Mao returned to the inner palace and summoned three men—Wang Chen, Palace Attendant; Wang Jing, Minister of the Secretariat; and Wang Ye, Regular Mounted Attendant—to deliberate with him in private. Cao Mao wept and said, “Sima Zhao’s treasonous ambition to usurp the throne is known to all! We will not sit still and submit to deposition and humiliation. You must help Us strike him down!” Wang Jing memorialized, “You must not. In former times, Duke Zhao of Lu could not endure the Ji clan, but was defeated, driven into exile, and lost his state. Now supreme power has long belonged to the Sima clan. Among the high ministers within and without the court, there is more than one who, heedless of right and wrong, fawns upon these wicked traitors. Moreover, Your Majesty’s palace guards are few and weak, and none among them can be relied upon to carry out your commands. If Your Majesty cannot endure this for the present, no calamity could be greater. For now you should proceed slowly and must not act rashly.” Cao Mao said, “If this can be endured, what cannot be endured? Our mind is made up. Even if We die, what is there to fear?” Having said this, he went in at once to inform the Empress Dowager. Wang Chen and Wang Ye said to Wang Jing, “The situation is now desperate. We must not bring upon ourselves the calamity of having our clans exterminated. We should go to Duke Sima’s residence and report the plot, thereby escaping death.” Wang Jing was furious and said, “When the sovereign is troubled, the minister is disgraced; when the sovereign is humiliated, the minister dies. How dare you harbor divided loyalties?” Seeing that Wang Jing would not comply, Wang Chen and Wang Ye went directly to report everything to Sima Zhao.

p.src: A short while later, Cao Mao, Emperor of Wei, emerged from the inner palace and ordered his guard Jiao Bo to assemble more than three hundred palace guards, servants, and young attendants in the audience hall. Raising a great clamor, they marched out. Cao Mao mounted his carriage with sword in hand and commanded his attendants to proceed straight out through the southern palace gate. Wang Jing prostrated himself before the carriage and, weeping bitterly, remonstrated: “Your Majesty, to lead a few hundred men against Sima Zhao is merely to drive sheep into a tiger’s jaws. To die for nothing will serve no purpose. Your servant does not cherish his own life; I truly believe only that this undertaking cannot succeed.” Cao Mao said, “Our troops are already on the march. Do not obstruct Us.” He then advanced toward the Dragon Gate.

p.src: Presently Jia Chong appeared in armor and on horseback, with Cheng Cui on his left and Cheng Ji on his right, leading several thousand armored imperial guards who came charging forward with battle cries. Cao Mao brandished his sword and shouted, “We are the Son of Heaven! You force your way into the palace grounds—do you mean to murder your sovereign?” When the imperial guards saw Cao Mao, none dared move. Jia Chong called to Cheng Ji, “For what purpose has Duke Sima maintained you? It was precisely for a day such as this.” Cheng Ji seized his halberd and, looking back at Jia Chong, asked, “Am I to kill him, or bind him?” Jia Chong said, “Duke Sima has given his order: he wants him dead.” Cheng Ji leveled his halberd and charged straight toward the imperial carriage. Cao Mao shouted, “How dare a common wretch show such insolence!” Before the words had left his mouth, Cheng Ji thrust his halberd into Cao Mao’s chest and knocked him out of the carriage. With a second thrust, the blade passed out through his back, and he died beside the carriage. Jiao Bo came at him with leveled spear, but Cheng Ji killed him with a single thrust of his halberd. Everyone else fled. Wang Jing came rushing after them and cursed Jia Chong: “Traitor! How dare you murder your sovereign?” Jia Chong was enraged. He ordered his men to bind Wang Jing securely and sent word to Sima Zhao. Sima Zhao entered the palace and, seeing Cao Mao already dead, feigned great shock. He struck his head against the imperial carriage and wept, then ordered that all the high ministers be informed.

p.src: At that time, Grand Tutor Sima Fu entered the palace. Seeing Cao Mao’s body, he pillowed the dead emperor’s head upon his lap and wept, saying, “That Your Majesty was murdered is this servant’s crime!” He placed Cao Mao’s body in an inner and outer coffin and laid it in state west of a side hall. Sima Zhao entered the hall and summoned all the ministers to deliberate. All the ministers arrived except Chen Tai, Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat. Sima Zhao ordered Chen Tai’s maternal uncle, Minister Xun Yi, to summon him. Chen Tai wept bitterly and said, “Commentators have compared me with my uncle, but today my uncle has proved truly inferior to me.” He put on hempen mourning garments, entered the palace, and prostrated himself weeping before the imperial bier. Sima Zhao also feigned tears and asked, “By what law should today’s affair be dealt with?” Chen Tai replied, “Only by beheading Jia Chong can you make even a small measure of amends to all under Heaven.” Sima Zhao pondered for a long while, then asked, “Consider the next-best course.” Chen Tai said, “There are only measures more severe than that. I know of none less severe.” Sima Zhao said, “Cheng Ji has committed monstrous treason. He shall be put to death by slow dismemberment, and his three clans exterminated.” Cheng Ji reviled Sima Zhao, crying, “The crime is not mine! It was Jia Chong who conveyed your command!” Sima Zhao ordered that his tongue be cut out first. To the moment of his death, Cheng Ji never ceased crying that he had been wronged. p.src: Grand Tutor Sima Fu petitioned that Cao Mao be buried with the rites due a king, and Sima Zhao consented. Jia Chong and the others urged Sima Zhao to accept Wei's abdication and ascend the imperial throne. Sima Zhao said, “In former days King Wen possessed two-thirds of the realm, yet remained a servant of Yin; therefore the sages called him supremely virtuous. Emperor Wu of Wei would not accept abdication from Han, just as I will not accept abdication from Wei.” From these words Jia Chong and the others understood that Sima Zhao intended the throne for his son Sima Yan, and they pressed him no further. In the sixth month of that year, Sima Zhao enthroned Cao Huang, Duke of Changdao District, as emperor, inaugurating the first year of the Jingyuan era. Cao Huang changed his name to Cao Huan; his courtesy name was Jingzhao. He was a grandson of Cao Cao, Emperor Wu, and the son of Cao Yu, Prince of Yan. Cao Huan invested Sima Zhao as Chancellor and Duke of Jin, and bestowed upon him one hundred thousand strings of cash and ten thousand bolts of silk. His many civil and military officials likewise received titles and rewards.

p.src: Spies soon carried the news into Shu. When Jiang Wei heard that Sima Zhao had murdered Cao Mao and enthroned Cao Huan, he rejoiced. “Now I once again have just cause to attack Wei.” He thereupon sent a letter into Wu, calling upon it to raise troops and punish Sima Zhao for regicide; meanwhile, having obtained the Latter Ruler's approval, he mobilized one hundred and fifty thousand troops and several thousand wagons, each fitted with a wooden chest; and appointed Liao Hua and Zhang Yi as vanguard commanders. Liao Hua was to take Ziwu Valley, Zhang Yi Luo Valley, and Jiang Wei himself Xie Valley; all three were to emerge and rendezvous before Mount Qi. The three armies advanced together, sweeping toward Mount Qi.

p.src: At the time Deng Ai was training his troops in his mountain camp. Hearing that the Shu armies were attacking by three routes, he assembled his generals to deliberate. Staff Officer Wang Guan said, “I have a plan that cannot be spoken aloud. I have written it here and respectfully submit it for the general's inspection.” Deng Ai took it, unfolded it, and after reading it laughed. “The plan is ingenious, but I fear it will not deceive Jiang Wei.” Wang Guan said, “I am willing to risk my life and go.” Deng Ai said, “If your resolve is firm, you will surely succeed.” He then assigned five thousand troops to Wang Guan. Wang Guan advanced through Xie Valley by night and ran straight into the scouts of the Shu vanguard. Wang Guan called out, “We are Wei soldiers come to surrender. Report this to your commander.”

p.src: The scouts informed Jiang Wei, who ordered the remaining troops detained and summoned only their leader before him. Wang Guan prostrated himself and said, “I am Wang Guan, nephew of Wang Jing. Recently Sima Zhao murdered his sovereign and put my uncle's entire household to death; I hate him to the marrow of my bones. Now, happily, you have raised an army to punish his crime, so I have specially brought the five thousand soldiers under my command to surrender. I beg to serve at your command and destroy the traitorous faction, thereby avenging my uncle.” Jiang Wei was delighted and said to Wang Guan, “Since you have come to surrender in all sincerity, how could I fail to treat you with equal sincerity? The only thing troubling my army is provisions. We now have grain and fodder at the mouth of the valley; you may transport it to Mount Qi. I shall go at once to seize the camp at Mount Qi.” Wang Guan rejoiced inwardly, believing Jiang Wei had fallen into the trap, and gladly accepted the order. Jiang Wei said, “You need not take all five thousand men to transport the grain. Lead three thousand there and leave two thousand to guide us in the attack on Mount Qi.” Fearing that Jiang Wei might grow suspicious, Wang Guan departed with three thousand troops. Jiang Wei ordered Fu Qian to take the two thousand Wei soldiers along on the campaign and employ them as needed. Suddenly word came that Xiahou Ba had arrived. Xiahou Ba said, “Commander, why did you trust Wang Guan's words? When I was in Wei, though I did not know every detail, I never heard that Wang Guan was Wang Jing's nephew. There is much deceit in this; I beg you to examine it closely.” Jiang Wei laughed. “I already knew Wang Guan's surrender was a trick. That is why I divided his strength and am turning his own stratagem against him.” Xiahou Ba said, “Pray explain it.” Jiang Wei said, “Sima Zhao is a treacherous hero comparable to Cao Cao. Having killed Wang Jing and exterminated three generations of his clan, how could he leave a close nephew alive beyond the passes and entrust him with troops? Thus I knew it was a trick. Your judgment, Zhongquan, secretly accorded with mine.”

p.src: Jiang Wei therefore did not emerge from Xie Valley, but secretly stationed men in ambush along the road to guard against Wang Guan's spies. Within ten days, the ambush duly captured the messenger whom Wang Guan had sent back to Deng Ai with a letter and brought him before Jiang Wei. Jiang Wei questioned him about the circumstances and found the secret letter. It arranged that on the twentieth day of the eighth month Wang Guan would convey the provisions back to the main camp by a side road, and asked Deng Ai to send troops to meet him in Tanshan Valley. Jiang Wei killed the messenger, then altered the letter to say the fifteenth day of the eighth month and to ask Deng Ai himself to lead a great army to meet them in Tanshan Valley. On the one hand, he sent a man disguised as a Wei soldier to deliver the letter to the Wei camp; on the other, he had several hundred existing provision wagons unloaded of grain and filled with dry firewood, thatch, and other combustibles, then covered with blue cloth. Fu Qian was ordered to lead the two thousand supposedly surrendered Wei troops, bearing the banners of a grain convoy. Jiang Wei and Xiahou Ba each led an army to lie in ambush in the valley. He ordered Jiang Shu to emerge from Xie Valley, while Liao Hua and Zhang Yi also advanced their forces to seize Mount Qi.

u.src: Jiang Wei therefore did not emerge from Xie Valley, but secretly stationed men in ambush along the road to guard against Wang Guan's spies.
Within ten days, the ambush duly captured the messenger whom Wang Guan had sent back to Deng Ai with a letter and brought him before Jiang Wei.

Jiang Wei questioned him about the circumstances and found the secret letter. It arranged that on the twentieth day of the eighth month Wang Guan would convey the provisions back to the main camp by a side road, and asked Deng Ai to send troops to meet him in Tanshan Valley.

p.src: Now Deng Ai, having received Wang Guan's letter, was overjoyed. He hastily wrote a reply and ordered the messenger to carry it back. On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, Deng Ai led fifty thousand picked troops straight toward Tanshan Valley. From afar he sent men to high ground to reconnoiter, and they saw countless provision wagons passing in an unbroken line through a hollow in the hills. Deng Ai reined in his horse and looked; they were indeed all Wei soldiers. His attendants said, “Night is falling. We should quickly meet Wang Guan and escort him out of the valley.” Deng Ai said, “The terrain ahead is obscured by the mountains. If there are troops in ambush, retreat will be difficult; we can only wait here.” As he spoke, two riders suddenly galloped up and reported, “General Wang has carried the provisions across the border, and enemy troops are pursuing from behind. He begs you to come swiftly to his aid.” Deng Ai was alarmed and urgently spurred his troops forward. It was then the first watch, and the moon shone as brightly as day. Hearing battle cries behind the mountain, he assumed Wang Guan was fighting there. But as he charged around the mountain, a body of troops suddenly burst from the woods. At their head was the Shu general Fu Qian, who urged his horse forward and shouted, “Deng Ai, you wretch! You have fallen into my commander's trap! Why do you not dismount at once and accept death?” Deng Ai was greatly alarmed, wheeled his horse about, and fled. The wagons all burst into flame. Those flames were the signal. The Shu troops poured out from both sides and shattered the Wei army into scattered fragments. All across the mountains they could hear the cry: “A thousand gold pieces and the title of Marquis of Ten Thousand Households to whoever captures Deng Ai!” Terrified, Deng Ai cast off armor and helmet, abandoned his mount, mingled among the infantry, and escaped by scrambling over mountains and ridges. Jiang Wei and Xiahou Ba watched only for the mounted leader and pressed forward to capture him, never imagining that Deng Ai had escaped on foot. Jiang Wei then led his victorious troops to take possession of Wang Guan's provision wagons.

p.src: Now Wang Guan had secretly made an agreement with Deng Ai and had prepared provisions, fodder, carts, and equipment ahead of time, waiting only for the plan to be set in motion. Suddenly, a trusted man reported, “The plan has been exposed. General Deng has suffered a crushing defeat, and no one knows whether he is alive or dead.” Wang Guan was greatly alarmed and sent scouts to investigate. They returned to report that troops were closing in to attack from three directions, while behind them great clouds of dust were rising; there was no way out on any side. Wang Guan shouted an order to his men to set fire to all the provisions, fodder, and wagons. In an instant flames leapt up, and the raging fire scorched the sky. Wang Guan cried out, “The situation is desperate! You must all fight to the death!” He then led his troops in a charge toward the west. Behind him, Jiang Wei’s three columns gave chase. Jiang Wei assumed that Wang Guan was risking his life to break back into Wei territory, never imagining that he would instead fight his way into Hanzhong. Because his force was small and he feared the pursuers would overtake him, Wang Guan burned down all the plank roads and every pass. Fearing that Hanzhong might be lost, Jiang Wei abandoned his pursuit of Deng Ai and led his troops through the night along a shortcut to hunt down Wang Guan. Attacked on every side by the Shu troops, Wang Guan threw himself into the Heilong River and died. Jiang Wei had all the remaining soldiers buried alive. Although Jiang Wei had defeated Deng Ai, he had lost a great quantity of provisions and fodder, and the plank roads had been destroyed; he therefore withdrew his army to Hanzhong. Deng Ai led his defeated men back to the camp at Mount Qi, submitted a memorial confessing his guilt, and voluntarily demoted himself. Since Sima Zhao knew that Deng Ai had repeatedly rendered great service, he could not bear to demote him and instead bestowed generous rewards upon him once more. Deng Ai distributed all the wealth he had originally been awarded among the families of the officers and soldiers who had perished. Fearing that the Shu army might come forth again, Sima Zhao sent another fifty thousand troops to help Deng Ai defend the frontier. Jiang Wei repaired the plank roads through the night and again discussed launching a campaign. Indeed:
